articles.headline: Alton Bluffs Still Shaking From Summer Blasts
articles.subhead: Quarry work near the river cracked foundations, rattled windows, and split open the limestone. Neighbors say things haven't been right since.
body: For three weeks in August, the windows on Alton's river road rattled every afternoon at two o'clock. The quarry upriver was blasting into the bluffs, and the people who live beneath them have been counting the damage ever since.

"Cracked my basement wall clean through," said a retired lock-and-dam worker whose house sits below the bluffs. "I've lived here forty years. You get used to the barges. You don't get used to the hill moving."

The quarry operator says the blasting was permitted and inspected, and that the work stopped on schedule. State geologists confirmed that one charge opened a fissure in the bluff face, exposing what appears to be a natural cave. The opening has been fenced off, and officials have asked hikers and climbers to stay away.

Residents say the fence isn't the problem. Since the blasting stopped, neighbors along the river road describe dogs that won't go outside after dark, a goose pen found empty one morning with the wire torn upward, and something heavy moving over the rooftops on calm nights. "Like a sail filling up," one woman said. "Then nothing."

A few miles away, tourists still stop to photograph the painted Piasa, the winged monster on the bluffs that Father Marquette wrote about in 1673. The painting is a modern recreation. The legend, everyone agrees, is only a legend.
The quarry's next blasting permit comes before the county board in November.
articles.marginalia: the geese weren't taken from the ground

articles.headline: Delivery Driver Vanishes on Cherokee Street
articles.subhead: His car was found with the engine running and the door open. His family wants to know why police aren't looking harder.
body: Joey made his last delivery on Cherokee Street a little after 10 p.m. on a Tuesday. The customer got her order. Joey never made it back to his car.

Officers found the vehicle the next morning, parked at the curb with the engine still running, the driver's door open, and his phone on the seat. There were no signs of a struggle. The 23-year-old's family says he had no reason to leave and nowhere to go.
"He's a good kid. He calls his mother every night," said an uncle who has organized volunteers to hand out flyers along the street. "Somebody on this block saw something. Somebody heard something."

A spokesman for the Third District said the case remains open but called it "a missing adult case with no evidence of foul play." The family is asking anyone who was on Cherokee Street that night to come forward.

articles.headline: The City Beneath the City
articles.subhead: Before refrigeration, St. Louis kept its beer cold underground. Most of those caves are still down there.
body: Walk Cherokee Street today and you are walking on a roof. Beneath South City runs a honeycomb of natural limestone caves that, in the 1800s, made St. Louis one of the brewing capitals of the world. German brewers stacked their lager casks in the constant chill underground, where the temperature hardly changes from January to July.

When artificial refrigeration arrived, the breweries moved on. The caves were filled, forgotten, or simply bricked off behind basement walls. Nobody knows exactly how many entrances remain. City records from the period are incomplete, and some of the oldest building plans show cellars that no longer appear on any later map.
Every few years a contractor knocks through a wall and finds one. The cool air, the old brickwork, and the occasional rusted relic make for good stories. Most are sealed again within the week.

articles.headline: Old Cathedral to Hold All Souls' Mass
body: The Basilica of St. Louis, King of France, will hold its traditional All Souls' Day Mass on November 2 at 7 p.m. The parish's lay brotherhood, the Confraternity of St. Joseph, will host a reception afterward in the rectory. Parishioners are reminded that the lower crypt remains closed to visitors for restoration work.

articles.headline: Arts Patrons Gather in the Central West End
body: Philanthropist Celeste Marchand opened her Lindell Boulevard home Saturday for the season's first benefit for the city's historic preservation fund. Guests noted the hostess's famous gloves, her famously dry toasts, and a generous pledge toward "protecting the places this city would rather forget."

blotter.text: Caller reports a phone ringing in an alley. Officers found no phone.
Groundskeeper reports a mausoleum door standing open. Door was locked when officers arrived. Groundskeeper insists he did not lock it.
Resident reports a man in a long coat standing under a streetlight, facing her house, for two hours. Gone on arrival. Third report this month.
Jogger reports every bird in the Grand Basin taking off at once, "like something scared them." No further action.
